detail.longDescription: in some ways, modern PL research is just as much the rightful heir to 20th century AI research as machine learning is. unification is an old AI algorithm(s, there's more than one of these, actually). yes, that means type inference is sorta AI, too. and while that may sound contrived at first, consider the supporting evidence: if a type system by clever construction can make certain guarantees about well-typed programs, then type inference isn't just a fancy autocomplete, it's an inference engine, a miniature expert system trying to advise you where bugs in your program might lurk. we don't often call this type of research "AI" anymore, and i'm not asking you to change that; but i do want to remember history, and in particular draw the connection that PL stuff is very much also vulnerable to this cycle of overpromising and then underdelivering that is also like this big pattern in the history of AI research. like, it's very easy to get carried away in all the possibilities of what type systems could do for us, and forget about all the really hard problems+annoyances along the way we have yet to solve. my plea here is for PL people (including me) to show restraint in what we promise, and not just leave the inconvenient parts we don't have solutions for yet out of discussions. the rust and haskell communities tend to do this, and it can be exhausting and turn some bright people away. like, what sold *me* on type systems (at least more complicated ones) was neither haskell nor rust, but learning about types as propositions. and unlike some other contemporary hype bubbles, there are actual things of value here that i don't wanna see get lost to some form of PL winter. # PL # PLTheory # AI # programming
